questions.prompt: In cache poisoning, what does the attacker need to match to get a forged reply accepted?
options: The query's question, its 16-bit ID, and (since 2008) its random source port

questions.prompt: Who showed in 2008 how to make DNS cache poisoning fast and reliable? (last name)
Why does DNS amplification work so well as a DDoS weapon?
options: A small query with a spoofed source address makes an open resolver send a much bigger reply to the victim
DNS servers have no bandwidth limits

questions.prompt: Resolvers should answer recursive queries from anyone on the Internet.
Security sees thousands of lookups for long, random names like `aGVsbG8gd29ybGQ.x7k2.net`. What's the likely cause?
options: DNS tunneling: data hidden in the query names

questions.prompt: What does DNSSEC add to DNS records: encryption or signatures? (one word)
With DNSSEC, people on the network can no longer see which names you look up.
Which record, kept in the parent zone, links a child zone's key into the chain of trust?
Which record holds a DNSSEC signature?
On which TCP port does DNS over TLS run? (a number)
